note: Wren Phonics — SEND guide (b410, 2026-10-08), built from research §1D/§3 and DfE criterion C14/footnote 1 in Wren's own words — no commercial SEND programme's specific resources are referenced or copied. provenance: Wren original, b410, 2026-10-08.
pace_and_routine: Slower, with more repetition, in a predictable routine the child comes to recognise — the same time, the same place, the same four-part shape (Warm up, New sound, Have a go, Use it) every session, just stretched out over more sessions and smaller steps within each one. Nothing about WHAT is taught changes; only the pace and the step size.
multi_sensory_practice: Every Wren Phonics grapheme already pairs a sound with a picture cue, an action and a formation cue (voice + picture + movement). For a child who needs more, add channels that keep the child's attention on the letters and sounds themselves: say the sound while feeling it (a hand on the throat for a voiced sound like m, v or z, a puff of air on the palm for p or t); build and change words with magnetic, foam or tile letters the child can hold and move, one letter or grapheme per sound; air-write a letter large, then write it once with a pencil on paper. Wren Phonics does not use sand, shaving foam, paint or dough letters for phonics: the DfE's validation guidance (Note 8) gives "finding letters in sand" as an example of an activity that makes children focus on something other than reading, and the Reading Framework (2023, p.55) says painting or making models of letters does not give enough practice in word reading. A child whose physical needs make pencil work very hard may need other ways to write — letter tiles, a keyboard or an adult scribe (Reading Framework p.79) — agreed with the SENCo. Trial any adaptation with the specific child it is for, since what helps one child does not automatically help another.
communication_aids: Common, generic classroom aids that work alongside this programme without changing it: large dice or spinners for choosing a sound to practise, small whiteboards and physical letters/tiles a child can move rather than write, phoneme frames (one box per sound in a word, moved into as it is said) for segmenting support, and a consistent set of flash cards matching exactly what has been taught so far — the same DfE footnote (C14, footnote 1) that names these as examples of "adapted approaches", not Wren inventions.
one_programme_not_a_different_one: A child with SEND learns to read through the same systematic synthetic phonics sequence as every other child in the setting — same GPCs, same order. SEND adaptation changes delivery (pace, group size, sensory channel, communication aid), never the content or the sequence, and a child is never moved onto a different reading scheme or strategy because of it.
small_group_or_1to1: Most SEND adaptation happens in a small group or 1:1, in a quiet space with fewer distractions, with more direct adult interaction than the whole-class lesson gives — the same quiet, consistent space Same-day boost uses works well here too.
speech_sound_needs: Speech sound difficulties: a child who cannot yet say a sound clearly can still learn which letters go with it. Accept the child's own consistent attempt at a sound, check what they know by asking them to point ("show me the one that says /s/" from two or three cards), and talk to the child's speech and language therapist so the phonics sounds and therapy targets support each other. Do not drill a sound the therapist says the child is not ready to say.
non_verbal_and_aac: Pre-verbal and non-verbal children, and children who use AAC: check blending without asking the child to say the word — say the sounds ("c-a-t") and ask them to point to the matching picture from two or three; check segmenting by having them choose letter tiles in order. The Reading Framework (pp.78-79) describes pupils selecting their response from auditory choices anchored to visual symbols, and low- or high-tech eye-gaze. Children who cannot give spoken answers do not take the Phonics Screening Check (see below), but they can still be taught and assessed this way.
hearing_impairment: Hearing impairment: sit the child close to the adult, facing them, with good light on the adult's face and as little background noise as possible; check that hearing aids or cochlear implant processors are working before the session; use the action and picture for every sound; and follow the advice of the child's Teacher of the Deaf. Cued Speech or visual phonics can help if they are used consistently, every day.
visual_impairment: Visual impairment: use the print size the child's qualified teacher of the visually impaired recommends (not just "bigger"), strong contrast, a clear font and uncluttered pages, and tactile letters if the child needs them. Braille users need specialist advice from the start.
graduated_approach: Use the SEND Code of Practice graduated approach — assess, plan, do, review — with the SENCo and the child's family, and record which adaptations you tried and whether they worked. Your local authority's Local Offer lists the SEND support available near you. In Ealing, for example, that is the Ealing Local Offer, and early years settings can apply to the Special Educational Needs Inclusion Fund (SENIF) for funded children who need extra support.

framework.name: Say it
framework.detail: Adult models the pure sound alone, 3 times. Child echoes each time before anything else happens — no letter, no picture yet, just the sound.

framework.name: See it
framework.detail: Show the grapheme together with its picture-cue mnemonic. Point to the grapheme while saying the sound again, so eye and ear connect to the same sound at the same moment.

framework.name: Feel it
framework.detail: Feel the sound being made (a hand on the throat for a voiced sound, a puff of air on the palm for p or t), then air-write the letter large and write it once with a pencil on paper, saying the sound each time — more repetitions than a mainstream lesson would use. Not sand, foam or dough: they pull attention away from the letter (DfE validation Note 8; Reading Framework p.55).

framework.name: Do it
framework.detail: Repeat the grapheme's own physical action several times, slowly at first, building speed only once the action itself is secure.

framework.name: Blend it
framework.detail: Blend the sound into exactly ONE already-known word, very slowly, sound-button by sound-button, before trying anything harder — do not introduce a second word until the first is secure.

framework.name: Check it
framework.detail: Child says the sound back correctly, unprompted, on request, at least 3 times across the session (not 3 times in a row at the end) before the session is counted as a pass.
